content.title: About
content.content: Black-eyed peas are a type of legume, also known as "cowpeas" or "southern peas." Originating from Africa, they are now widely cultivated in the United States, especially in the South. The small, light‑green seeds have a distinctive black spot, offering a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a tender texture when cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In the Southern United States black-eyed peas are considered a symbol of good luck and are traditionally served on New Year's Day.
A classic Southern dish called "Hoppin' John" combines black-eyed peas with rice and seasonings.
The plant is a nitrogen‑fixing legume, improving soil fertility when rotated with other crops.
Dried seeds can be stored for up to a year in a cool, dry environment.
Black-eyed peas have been used in traditional African medicine to support digestion.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked black-eyed peas provides about 13 g of protein, making it a valuable protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are important for blood formation and anemia prevention, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Black-eyed peas raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytochemicals such as polyphenols help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes, including black-eyed peas.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: The seeds contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting mitigates this effect.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes can cause flatulence in sensitive people; gradual introduction to the diet can lessen the issue.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Black-eyed peas can be boiled, stewed, added to soups, salads, casseroles, and chili. They are also used in vegetarian patties and spreads. Soaking the dry peas for 4–6 hours, draining, and then cooking for 45–60 minutes yields a tender result.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried peas in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Cooked peas keep in the refrigerator for 4‑5 days or can be frozen for up to 3 months.

fish-catfish-baked-or-broiled-coated.title: Fish, catfish, baked or broiled, coated

content.title: About
content.content: Catfish fillet is a tender white meat that is commonly baked or broiled after being coated in a seasoned breadcrumb mixture. The result is a crispy crust surrounding moist, mildly sweet fish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Catfish are often farm‑raised, making them an affordable and sustainable protein source.
Coating typically combines flour, breadcrumbs, herbs, and spices for a flavorful crust.
Baking retains more nutrients, while broiling creates a deeper golden crust.
Catfish is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart and brain health.
The dish is traditionally served with lemon wedges, fresh herbs, or a light yogurt‑based sauce.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Catfish fillet provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Contains EPA and DHA, which help maintain cardiovascular and cognitive function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium, and potassium, beneficial for bones and nerve function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, catfish has a modest amount of saturated fat.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to catfish.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: While farmed catfish are usually monitored, choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Excess sodium
items.content: Using a salty coating can increase sodium intake, which may affect blood pressure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the coated catfish fillet as a main course with vegetables, potatoes, or rice. It also works well in sandwiches, salads, or cut into bite‑size pieces for appetizers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Smoked fish is fish that has undergone a cold or hot smoking process, giving it a distinctive aroma, firm texture, and extended shelf life. Commonly smoked species include salmon, herring, mackerel, and trout.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Smoking has been used for over 5,000 years as a method of food preservation.
Smoked fish retains high levels of omega‑3 fatty acids even after heat treatment.
The tradition of smoked fish is especially strong in Scandinavian countries, where it is called “røkt fisk.”
Different woods (oak, cherry, alder) impart unique flavors and aromas to the fish.
Smoked fish is often served as an appetizer, in salads, or as a sandwich filling.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Smoked fish provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health, lower triglyceride levels, and have anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for nervous system function and energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Smoked fish supplies selenium, iodine, and phosphorus, which aid thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Makes it suitable for low‑carb and keto diets.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Smoked fish is often salty; people with hypertension should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Potential heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Some fish species can accumulate mercury; choose reputable suppliers.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to seafood may react to smoked fish.

items.title: Bacterial risk if improperly smoked
items.content: If smoking is done at too low a temperature, pathogenic bacteria may survive.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Smoked fish can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to salads, pastas, rice or potato dishes, used in sandwiches, or as a filling for sushi rolls. Before eating, you may rinse off excess salt under cold water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store smoked fish in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 5‑7 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a sealed bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Check for off‑odors or slimy texture before consumption; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.

green-peas-canned-cooked-fat-added-ns-as.title: Green peas, canned, cooked, fat added, NS as to fat type

content.title: About
content.content: Canned green peas are cooked pea beans packed in a sealed tin with added vegetable oil. The product is ready to eat, retains a bright green color and a tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas belong to the legume family and are a good source of plant protein.
Canning allows the peas to be stored for several years without major loss of nutrients.
The added fat enhances flavor and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Peas are used in traditional dishes worldwide, from soups to purees.
Cans are often marked with the NS code, indicating that the type of fat is not specified.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of canned peas provides about 8 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas are high in B1, B6 and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: The combination of plant fats and potassium contributes to normal blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in peas help combat free radicals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; people monitoring sodium should check the label.

items.title: Added fat type unknown
items.content: The fat type is not specified (NS), so those with specific fat restrictions should be cautious.

items.title: Bacterial contamination after opening
items.content: Once opened, the product should be refrigerated and consumed within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, stews, or blended into a puree. For extra flavor, toss with herbs, spices, or a splash of lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the peas in a sealed container in the refrigerator and use within 3‑4 days.

hot-dog-sandwich-turkey-on-white-bread.title: Turkey Hot Dog Sandwich on White Bread

content.title: About
content.content: The turkey hot dog sandwich is a handheld meal that replaces the traditional pork sausage with cooked turkey meat, served inside a soft white bread roll. It offers a familiar hot‑dog experience with a lighter protein source.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey contains less fat than typical pork hot‑dog sausages, making this version lower in calories.
White bread provides a soft texture but less fiber than whole‑grain alternatives.
The classic hot dog originated in the United States in the early 1900s; turkey variants gained popularity in the 1990s as a healthier option.
The sandwich is portable and requires no utensils, ideal for on‑the‑go meals.
Many recipes add barbecue sauce or mustard to enhance the flavor of the turkey.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Turkey is a rich source of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with pork hot‑dog meat, turkey provides less saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium in turkey helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides quick energy
items.content: The combination of protein and carbohydrates from the bread delivers fast and sustained energy.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to bird meat, including turkey.

items.title: High glycemic index of white bread
items.content: White bread can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, which may be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared turkey often contains added salt; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Preservatives in processed meat
items.content: Some ready‑to‑eat turkey products contain nitrites or other preservatives that should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is eaten by hand like any hot dog. It can be warmed in a microwave or on a grill, and topped with fresh vegetables, lettuce, mustard, ketchup, or barbecue sauce to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared sandwich refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze it and reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

kidney-beans-from-canned-no-added-fat.title: Canned Kidney Beans, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Canned kidney beans are a fully cooked, ready‑to‑eat product made from selected bean varieties that are boiled until tender and sealed in an airtight can without any added fats. The beans retain their nutty flavor, firm texture, and a rich profile of nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kidney beans are also known as red beans and are a staple in Latin American, Mediterranean, and Asian cuisines.
Canning preserves most B‑vitamins and minerals while extending shelf life to several years.
The deep red color comes from anthocyanin antioxidants.
Unlike many canned foods, this product contains no added oils, making it a low‑calorie option.
Kidney beans are a popular plant‑based protein source for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 8 g of plant protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron contributes to hemoglobin formation, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fats makes this product suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals such as anthocyanins help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytates, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; monitor intake if you need to limit sodium.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Raw kidney beans contain lectins that are toxic, but the canning process destroys them completely.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add the beans to salads, soups, chili, stews, or use them as a filling for tacos and burritos. They can be quickly heated in the microwave or on the stovetop, and seasoned with herbs, spices, or a splash of lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the beans in the refrigerator in the original or an airtight container for 3–4 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Sunflower seeds (NFS) are edible seeds of the sunflower (Helianthus annuus) cultivated for food purposes. They have a light nutty flavor, crunchy texture, and are commonly eaten raw, roasted, or salted.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sunflower is one of the fastest‑growing annual crops, reaching up to 3 m in height.
The seeds contain over 40 % healthy fats, most of which are polyunsaturated.
Sunflower was domesticated in North America more than 5,000 years ago.
Seeds are widely used to produce oil, one of the most popular vegetable oils worldwide.
Seeds are available unsalted, salted, or flavored with various spices.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Polyunsaturated fatty acids support heart health.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Seeds supply plant protein and dietary fiber, promoting satiety.

items.title: Contains phytosterols
items.content: Phytosterols may help lower blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to sunflower seeds.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salted varieties can contribute to excessive sodium intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Seeds are energy‑dense, so they should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large amounts may cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sunflower seeds can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, yogurts, granola, baked goods, or used as a topping. They can also be roasted or baked with various seasonings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.

white-pizza-cheese-with-meat-and-vegetab.title: White pizza with cheese, meat and vegetables, thick crust

content.title: About
content.content: White pizza is made without tomato sauce; instead a creamy cheese sauce is used. Topped with a variety of meats (ham, chicken, beef) and fresh vegetables (bell pepper, mushrooms, onion). The crust is thick, soft and airy, making the dish hearty and flavorful.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White pizza gained popularity in the United States in the early 1920s as an alternative to classic Margherita.
The creamy sauce is often prepared from ricotta, mozzarella and cream, giving a delicate taste.
Thick crusts are traditionally baked in stone ovens where temperatures reach 300 °C, creating a crisp outer layer and a fluffy interior.
The combination of meat and vegetables provides a balanced source of protein, vitamins, and minerals.
In some regions fresh basil or arugula is added after baking for a bright, fresh note.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat toppings supply high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium, while cheese contributes calcium and vitamin D.

items.title: Energy density
items.content: Thick crust and cheese provide lasting satiety through complex carbs and fats.

items.title: Probiotic effect
items.content: Certain cheeses (e.g., mozzarella) contain live cultures that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Vegetables such as bell pepper and mushrooms are rich in antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The thick crust and cheese make the pizza calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Creamy sauce and cheese contain saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Salt and preservatives
items.content: Processed meats like sausage and ham often contain salt and nitrites; people with hypertension should choose lower‑salt options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cut into slices. Optionally sprinkle fresh herbs (basil, oregano) or a drizzle of olive oil just before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore a crispy crust.
